title: Al-Kabir, the Most Great
tomorrow: who guards the people you love when you can't?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-'Aliyy, praised with your forehead on the floor. The line: most high. Today, two words that open every prayer, and a question they leave hanging.
screen: `MOST HIGH.` → `TWO WORDS THAT OPEN THE PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Best pizza in the city. Best player ever. Best album of the year. Those arguments never end, because every comparison needs something to compare against, and someone always brings a new one. Yesterday's question: Allahu akbar, greater than what, exactly? It's the sentence that opens the Muslim prayer, said with the hands raised. Allah is greater. And then the sentence just stops.
screen: `BEST EVER, ACCORDING TO WHO?` → `ALLAHU AKBAR.` → `AND THEN IT STOPS.`

segments.voice: That stop is the point. Nothing comes after greater. Teachers often explain the empty space like this: greater than whatever you'd put there. Your fear, your plans, the best thing you've ever seen. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said that the prayer's sacred state begins with takbir, saying Allahu akbar, and ends with the salam. Everything outside is set aside with two words. Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight: you can't put anything after akbar that makes it smaller. That's today's Name. Al-Kabir, the Most Great, which the Qur'an pairs with the Most High: the one who knows the hidden and the seen, the Great, the Exalted. Now a neighbor. Jews and Christians sing and pray the Psalms, and Psalm one hundred forty-five says, in the King James words: "Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; and his greatness is unsearchable." That's a shared instinct, in their own words: a greatness no one can measure to the end. And an honest difference. The Psalm is a song that keeps going, praise line after praise line. The takbir is two words that open a prayer and then fall silent. Two ways of saying a greatness has no edge, and neither needs to borrow the other's.
screen: `NOTHING COMES AFTER GREATER.` · `THE PRAYER OPENS WITH TAKBIR.` · `PSALM 145: UNSEARCHABLE.` · `A SONG, AND TWO WORDS.` · then, large: `GREATER.`

segments.voice: Say it once out loud, slowly: Allahu akbar, or simply its meaning in English, greater. Leave a beat of silence after it. Into that silence, set the biggest thing on your mind today, and let the word stay bigger than it through the sit.
Al-Kabir. The Most Great, said in a sentence that stops at greater and lets nothing in after.
Carry this: greater, with nothing after it, whatever today tries to put there. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims open each prayer with Allahu akbar, hands raised, and say it at many other moments: the call to prayer, the days of Eid, and on seeing something awe-inspiring.

fork.setup: your little brother asks at dinner, 'if God is greater, greater than WHAT?' what's a sentence you could give him?
options: 'greater than anything you could put after it. that's why it stops.'
'it's just something people say; don't think about it too hard.'
'greater than the biggest thing, like the sun or the ocean.'
fork.reveal: any one thing you name makes it a contest. the sentence stops at greater so nothing can be put after it.

original.note: Arabic: the Most Great. the takbir says akbar: greater.

trapdoor: what you thought: Allahu akbar is a slogan.
what it means: Allah is greater, with the comparison left open, so nothing can be set beside Him; the words that open the prayer.
